title: The weights, and what they cost to move
kicker: 09 · The weights, and what they cost to move

scenes.name: the whole model, and where it can sit
scenes.visual: One continuous shot in two stages. Stage 1 (b1–b2), centre: an equation that builds term by term, written in the order it is worked: 'parameter count × bytes per parameter = memory' ('parameter count' blue, 'bytes per parameter' and 'memory' coral, operators white). The worked line sits directly beneath it, each piece under its own term: '70 B' under 'parameter count', '× 2 bytes' under 'bytes per parameter', '= 140 GB' under 'memory'. The numbers live only in the worked line, never inside the equation. Lower right: a small amber square 'chip' and, beside it, an empty coral-outlined container 'memory beside the chip'. Stage 2 (b3–b5): the equation shrinks to a one-line strip at top-left, '70 B × 2 bytes = 140 GB', and a three-row timing chart fills the frame under the header 'Fetching 140 GB from each place'. Row icons down the left third: a hard-drive icon 'disk'; the coral container from stage 1, relabelled 'memory beside the chip · H100'; the amber chip square, relabelled 'the chip itself' (held at 40% until b4). In b3 only, a grey what-if tag sits under row 2's label. The right two thirds hold one shared linear time axis, 0 to 20 s across 1,200 px, ticks every 5 s, faint grey, tagged 'same scale'. Row 1 gets a full-width coral bar; row 2 a coral sliver 2.5 px wide, truly to scale, shown under a magnifier; row 3 gets no bar. Each beat below says what dims or leaves, so no more than five text items besides numbers are bright at once. The idea: one block of bytes, three places it could be fetched from, and only the middle one both holds it and is fast.

beats.say: You have met this conversion: seventy billion parameters, at two bytes each, make a hundred and forty gigabytes.
beats.show: Opens on '70.6 B parameters' exactly as the previous chapter left it: blue, with an amber outline, as the numerator of a fraction bar with a blank denominator, and a '×' slot waiting beside it. The fraction bar, its blank denominator and the amber outline dissolve; the '×' slot stays attached to the number. The equation 'parameter count × bytes per parameter = memory' draws on across the upper centre, and the number, carrying its '×' slot, drops into the worked line beneath it, directly under 'parameter count'. On 'seventy billion', the number rounds to '70 B' and a grey side note at the right keeps the exact count: '70.6 B × 2 = 141.2 GB ≈ 140'. On 'two bytes', the waiting '×' slot fills to read '× 2 bytes', directly under 'bytes per parameter', with a small grey tag '16-bit'. On 'a hundred and forty gigabytes', coral '= 140 GB' lands at the end of the worked line, under 'memory'.

beats.say: That is the entire model, off the chip in the memory beside it, the same for every request.
beats.show: The side note dims to 30%. On 'entire model', the coral '140 GB' swells into a solid coral block and slides down-right into the empty container beside the amber 'chip' square. Three tags arrive one at a time on their words, each dimming to 40% as the next lands: 'the entire model', 'off the chip', 'same for every request'. Takeaway band: 'all of it beside the chip, none on it'.

beats.say: One last look at the disk. From a fast drive, fetching it all takes about twenty seconds, twenty thousand milliseconds. From the memory beside an H one hundred, if it fitted, about forty-two milliseconds: roughly five hundred times faster.
beats.show: As the beat begins, the three tags and the takeaway band leave, the equation, worked line and side note shrink into the one-line strip at top-left, the header 'Fetching 140 GB from each place' draws on, and the container and the chip square slide left to become the row-2 and row-3 icons with their labels; row 3's label stays at 40% until the next beat. On 'disk', the hard-drive icon fades in as the row-1 icon, label 'disk', and the time axis draws on with its 'same scale' tag. On 'fast drive', row 1's coral bar starts to grow, with a small grey tag 'time-lapse', and the strip and the 'same scale' tag dim to 30%. The bar reaches the 20 s mark on 'twenty seconds', grey '≈ 7 GB/s' at its end; on 'twenty thousand milliseconds', white 'about 20,000 ms' lands beside it and 'time-lapse' dims to 30%. On 'if it fitted', a small grey tag lands under row 2's label: 'what-if: pretend it fits on one H100'. On 'forty-two milliseconds', row 2's sliver appears in a blink with grey '3.35 TB/s' and white 'about 42 ms', and a magnifier circle pops over it to show it enlarged. On 'five hundred times', the '≈ 7 GB/s' and '3.35 TB/s' tags dim to 30%, the magnifier closes, and an amber bracket joins rows 1 and 2 at the right with '20 s ÷ 41.8 ms ≈ 478×', which morphs in place into 'roughly 500×'. Bright text besides numbers never exceeds four items: header, 'disk', row 2's label, the what-if tag.

beats.say: And from the chip itself? Not slow, but impossible. It holds about a tenth of a gigabyte in all.
beats.show: The bracket and its text leave. Rows 1 and 2 dim to 25% and their time, rate and what-if tags leave. On 'chip itself', row 3's label 'the chip itself' brightens to full, so row 3 is the focus. On 'not slow', a grey tag 'no bar' sits at the start of row 3. On 'impossible', a coral block '140 GB' slides along row 3 toward a tiny blue box at the axis origin and stops dead against it, unable to enter; the 'no bar' tag becomes white 'it does not fit'. On 'a tenth of a gigabyte', the box's label lands, '≈ 0.1 GB, whole chip', with a smaller grey tag under it, 'a few hundred KB per working area', and coral '> 1,000× too big' beside the stalled block.

beats.say: That's why the model is loaded once, and stays. Disk speeds vary widely, but the gap stays enormous. The disk explains only slow start-ups, and why nobody streams weights from storage.
beats.show: Row 3's block and tags leave and the row dims; rows 1 and 2 return to full with their 'about 20,000 ms' and 'about 42 ms' labels. On 'loaded once', a teal arrow 'load once' sweeps from the disk icon down into the container in row 2. On 'vary widely', a grey caveat tag under row 1: 'disk figures approximate, vary by hardware'; on 'stays enormous', a small amber 'roughly 500×' glows once between the two rows. On 'slow start-ups', row 1 turns grey, gains the tag 'start-up only', and slides off the left edge trailing 'after the load: never again'. Row 2's container brightens and glides to centre, where the next scene picks it up.

scenes.name: close and wide: what the memory beside the chip is
scenes.visual: Opens from the coral container at centre. Main element: the GPU package illustration (S.gpu, three stack sites per side) seen from above, centred and large: a blue slab, the amber die at centre, coral stacks left and right. The view changes twice, always by 2D camera zoom and crossfade, never by 3D rotation: in b2 the camera zooms into one stack and its plan-view rectangle crossfades into a side-elevation drawing of eight thin coral layers with fine vertical lines through them; in b3 the whole top view crossfades into a side elevation of the package: a long blue slab along the bottom, one coral stack at left and the amber die at right, a small gap between them, and a dense fan of hair-thin coral lines across the slab. From 'close, and wide' at the end of b3 and through b4, a small inset at top-right shows a laptop board in the same side elevation for comparison. In this scene 'slab' always means the package base the memory and the die both sit on, never the die itself. One header line across the top is replaced on each change, never stacked: 'not faster wires', 'close and wide', 'wide needs short', 'a placement, not a technology'. Colour by meaning: amber for the chip itself, the compute die, coral for the memory and the bits on its wires, blue for the package and the slab.

beats.say: Here is the package, carrying chip and memory together. At its centre, the chip itself: the compute die, one piece of silicon.
beats.show: The container grows into the package top view with its six stack sites still empty outlines. On 'package', label on the blue slab: 'one package'. On 'chip itself', the amber rectangle at the centre pulses, label 'the chip'; on 'compute die', a small grey '= compute die' lands beside it, as in the earlier chapter. On 'one piece of silicon', the amber rectangle flashes once.

beats.say: Around it, the stacks: memory dies, bonded one on another. The H one hundred has five, eighty gigabytes in all.
beats.show: On 'Around it', five sites fill coral in quick succession; the sixth fills as a dimmed solid grey stack tagged 'sixth stack, not enabled'. On 'memory dies', the camera zooms into the front-left stack and its plan-view rectangle crossfades into a side elevation; on 'bonded one on another', eight thin coral layers stack upward one by one, the top three labelled 'die', fine vertical lines drawing down through all eight, tag '8 dies × 2 GB = 16 GB'. On 'has five', the camera pulls back and the elevation crossfades back into the top view; the five coral stacks light in turn while a counter steps '16, 32, 48, 64, 80 GB'. On 'eighty gigabytes', a small spec card 'Memory capacity: 80 GB' slides in beside the package and ticks.

beats.say: Why call it high bandwidth memory, H B M? Not because each wire is faster. It sits millimetres away on the same package, joined by those five thousand one hundred and twenty wires: close, and wide.
beats.show: The spec card, the 'sixth stack' tag, and the 'the chip' label with its '= compute die' tag leave. On 'high bandwidth memory', a white label lands across the five stacks: 'HBM · high bandwidth memory', the same label as in the earlier chapter. On 'Not because', header 'not faster wires', and one grey tag under the slab: 'per wire: about a laptop's speed'. On 'It sits', the top view crossfades into the side elevation: blue slab, coral stack left now labelled just 'HBM', amber die right. On 'millimetres away', a dimension arrow 'millimetres' spans the gap. On 'those five thousand', a dense fan of hair-thin coral lines draws across the slab with the counter '5 × 1,024 = 5,120 wires', and coral particles flow along all of them at once; the per-wire tag leaves. On 'close', the header becomes 'close and wide' and the inset draws on at top-right: a laptop board in the same side elevation, coral memory module and amber processor 'centimetres' apart. On 'wide', the inset's sparse band of wires draws on, tag '128 wires', and amber '40×' lands between inset and main view.

beats.say: As you saw, wide needs short. Thousands of wires must be hair-thin, and thin wires carry a clean signal only over millimetres, so the memory cannot move further out and grow.
beats.show: Header 'wide needs short', the same label as in the earlier chapter. The camera zooms (2D) on the fan. On 'Thousands of wires', the '5,120 wires' counter pulses once; on 'hair-thin', the lines narrow further and crisp square coral pulses run along them. On 'only over millimetres', one thin wire stretches out to the inset's 'centimetres' and its square pulse smears into a soft blurred wave, grey tag 'high and low blur'; it snaps back, and the inset and '40×' dim to 30%. On 'cannot move further out', a grey hand cursor drags the stack away from the die; the fan stretches, frays and turns grey; the stack snaps back and the wires turn coral again.

beats.say: The name describes a placement, not a technology. The price is memory that is small and expensive.
beats.show: The camera pulls back to the full side elevation; the inset, the blur tag and the dimension arrow leave. Header 'a placement, not a technology'. On 'small', a pair of bars to scale under the package: a coral bar '80 GB · one H100' and, above it, a coral outline '140 GB · the model' overhanging it by 60 GB, grey tag 'more than one chip: later in the series'. On 'expensive', a price-tag icon appears beside the stack. Takeaway band: 'close and wide · small and expensive'.

scenes.name: read, never written
scenes.visual: One continuous composition across the frame, left to right: at left a coral block '140 GB of weights' (the memory beside the chip) with a small lock icon on its corner; across the left-centre the bus, a thick band of hair-thin coral lines; centre-right the amber chip; at the far right two user icons, one above the other, each joined to the chip by a thin blue line. Header across the top: 'The weights are read, never written', with a grey sub-line 'nothing about them changes while the service runs'. From b4 a small blue box '≈ 0.1 GB' sits inside the chip: the same tenth of a gigabyte the first scene showed. Nothing clears: elements dim, brighten or grow. The end state grows out of the same picture: a teal arrow from the block to the users and a coral arrow along the bus, then a push-in on the bus. Colour by meaning: coral for every movement of the weights, amber for the chip, blue for the users' questions and answers, teal for the consequence that helps.

beats.say: While the service runs, the weights are only read, never written: copied out, never changed. Training rewrote them at every step. Serving leaves them exactly as they were.
beats.show: Header and sub-line draw on; the coral block fades in at left. On 'only read', a coral arrow lifts a copy of one small tile out of the block; the block is unchanged. On 'never written', a pencil icon hovers over the block. On 'copied out', a label lands under the arrow: 'read = copy out'. On 'never changed', a label lands under the pencil, 'write = change'; the pencil is crossed out in grey and the lock clicks shut. On 'Training', the two labels dim to 40% and a small grey inset appears at bottom-left: 'training: rewritten every step'; on 'Serving', a white line under it: 'serving: read only'.

beats.say: Two users, two questions, the same hundred and forty gigabytes doing both jobs. So one copy serves everybody, which later makes batching possible: many users per pass.
beats.show: The read and write labels and the inset leave; the sub-line dims to 30%. The bus and the amber chip draw on to the right of the block; the two users slide in at the far right with bubbles 'weather tomorrow?' and 'fix my code'. Each question travels as a small blue pill along its line into the chip, and the bubbles shrink away. Coral streams flow from the block across the bus into the chip, flashing amber there, and small blue answer pills travel back out to each user. The block never changes. On 'the same hundred and forty gigabytes', a two-line tag under the block: 'the same 140 GB,' over 'for every request from every user'. On 'one copy serves everybody', that tag morphs into teal 'one copy serves everyone' and a faint teal outline wraps the block and both users. On 'batching', both users' blue pills enter the chip together on one coral stream; small grey tag 'batching: later'.

beats.say: The other side: every forward pass moves all one hundred and forty gigabytes across that bus, into the arithmetic units.
beats.show: The users, their pills and the batching tag dim to 30%; the teal outline and tag stay faint. The bus brightens. Tag above the bus: 'every forward pass'. On 'every forward pass', a coral packet '140 GB' crosses from the block into the chip, where it flashes amber and vanishes; a token counter above the chip ticks 'token 1'. On 'one hundred and forty gigabytes', the next identical packet crosses for 'token 2'; on 'arithmetic units', a third for 'token 3', each crossing taking exactly the same time. Small grey tag under the chip: 'at most ≈ 24 a second · H100 what-if'. Grey footnote along the bottom edge: 'strictly ≈ 139 GB: embedding rows are only gathered'.

beats.say: That is pure overhead, paid again and again. Nothing is learned, or saved, by having fetched the weights before.
beats.show: The rate tag and the footnote leave. As the beat begins, the small blue box '≈ 0.1 GB' appears inside the chip, and the next packet arrives as one long ribbon of small coral slices, labelled once, statically, along its length: 'layer 1', 'layer 2', '… layer 80'. The slices pass through the box a few at a time, each dropped out of the far side as the next arrives. On 'again and again', the layer labels fade and the time-lapse begins: plain packets cross faster and faster, grey tag 'time-lapse', the token counter speeds up and a coral running total under the bus climbs, stopping at '500 tokens → 70 TB'. On 'or saved', the counter ticks once more and a fresh ribbon sets off across the bus from the block, exactly as before.

beats.say: Two consequences, pointing opposite ways. One copy serves everyone, yet the same bytes are fetched every single time. The memory is close, but close is not the same as on, and every token pays for that trip.
beats.show: The running total and the 'time-lapse' tag leave. On 'one copy serves everyone', a large teal arrow grows from the block toward the two users, which brighten, label 'one copy serves everyone'. On 'fetched every single time', a large coral arrow grows along the bus into the chip, label 'the same bytes, fetched every token'. On 'not the same as on', both arrow labels dim to 40% and the camera pushes in on the bus between the block and the chip until the gap fills the centre of the frame and glows coral. On 'every token pays', the glowing gap pulses once. Takeaway band: 'close and wide, but not on the die'. Hold.

checks.claim: Fig 105: 70 billion parameters × 2 bytes = 140,000,000,000 bytes = 140 GB
Fig 105 reconciled with ch08's exact count (on screen, s01.b1 side note): 70.6 B × 2 bytes = 141.2 GB ≈ 140; the film keeps the round 140 GB
Fig 106: disk row 'about 20,000 ms' implies about 7 GB/s (a fast NVMe drive, illustrative, matching ch02): 140 GB / 7 GB/s = 20 s = 20,000 ms
Fig 106: memory beside the chip on an H100, 140 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 41.8 ms, 'about 42 ms'

Fig 106 (on screen, s01.b3 bracket): '20 s ÷ 41.8 ms ≈ 478×', which morphs into the atlas's 'roughly 500×'. Replaces the earlier on-screen '20,000 ÷ 42 ≈ 476×'. CHAPTER_NOTES and ch02 give 479×, computed from the unrounded 41.79 ms (478.6); with the 41.8 shown on screen the quotient is 478.5, so the bracket says 478 so a viewer who divides gets the same answer
Fig 106 storyboard: on a 1,200 px axis for 20 s, the 41.8 ms bar is 2.5 px wide (truly to scale, shown under a magnifier)

CORRECTION to fig 106 'the chip holds a few hundred kilobytes': true per working area (an H100 SM has 256 KB registers + 256 KB L1/shared), but the whole chip holds 132 × 512 KB + 50 MB L2 ≈ 0.12 GB, shown as '≈ 0.1 GB, whole chip' to match ch02 and ch06. 140 GB is ≈ 1,150× that (1,400× against a flat 0.1 GB); either way '> 1,000× too big'

s01.b5 'Disk speeds vary widely, but the gap stays enormous' (replaces 'but the gap does not', which was false: the ratio moves with disk speed). From a 14 GB/s PCIe 5 drive to a 0.5 GB/s SATA drive, the H100's 3.35 TB/s is still 239× to 6,700× faster; 140 GB takes 10 s to 280 s off disk
Fig 105/107 (added, published H100 spec, on screen): each HBM3 stack is 8 dies × 2 GB = 16 GB; 5 stacks × 16 GB = 80 GB, the spec-sheet capacity
Fig 105/107 (added, matches ch06): 5 stacks × 1,024 wires = a 5,120-wire bus
Fig 107 'not faster memory chips' (matches ch06): 3.35 TB/s over 5,120 wires = 5.23 Gbit/s per wire, about a laptop's ≈ 6 Gbit/s; shown as one shared tag 'per wire: about a laptop's speed'
Fig 107 (added, matches ch06, on screen): 5,120 wires vs a laptop's 128 = 40×

Fig 107 'small' (added, matches ch02/ch06, on screen in s02.b5): the 140 GB model is 1.75× one H100's 80 GB, overhanging it by 60 GB; this is why s01.b3's 42 ms row carries the tag 'what-if: pretend it fits on one H100'

Fig 105 'reads all 140 GB' reconciled with ch07's embedding exception (on-screen footnote, s03.b3, 'strictly ≈ 139 GB: embedding rows are only gathered'): the embedding table is 128,256 × 8,192 × 2 = 2.10 GB and only a few of its rows are gathered, so strictly 141.2 − 2.1 ≈ 139 GB streams each pass (the output projection is still read in full); the round 140 stands
Fig 108 (added, on screen, ch02's figure): on an H100 the weights can cross the bus at most 3.35 TB/s / 140 GB = 23.9 times a second, '≈ 24 a second'
Fig 108 (added, on screen, matches ch04): a 500-token answer fetches 500 × 140 GB = 70 TB
